_comment: Neutral go->rust rule pack. Package-local mirror of the forever home
specs/port-rules/lang/go-rust/**; the engine reads only what is here.
Rule order in `rules` IS the transform order, and `precedence` must agree with it — the
loader refuses a pack where the two disagree rather than silently obeying one of them.
type_map is keyed by TYPE IDENTITY, not by spelling: a primitive by its bare name, a named
type by `package.Name`. The two cannot collide because a qualified key always carries a dot
a bare name may not. A named type this map does not carry, from a unit the corpus also
translates, resolves through that unit's emitted module instead — which is the case a
spelling table could not express at all.
type_constructors answers for a COMPOSITE by its constructor rather than its shape. One
`slice` entry answers every slice; a spelling table needed a row per element type.
type_map_overrides: one source type does not always take one target type. `string` becomes
an owned String where a value is stored — a field, a parameter, a return — and CANNOT be one
in a constant, because a Rust const must be known at compile time and String is
heap-allocated. Recording that here rather than branching on it keeps the decision reviewable.
pointer_dispositions decide what a pointer BECOMES, from facts the front end observed, in
declared order with the first match winning. Go is garbage-collected, so a `*T` says nothing
about ownership; the decision has to be made and it has to be recorded. Order matters: the
two conservative rules come first, so an escaping or unanalysed pointer never reaches a
borrow rule. There is deliberately NO catch-all — facts nothing accepts refuse, because an
invented default is a decision nobody wrote down.
copy_types names the SOURCE types whose target counterpart copies, keyed by source identity
the same way type_map is, so the two tables answer for the same thing. Reading anything else
by value MOVES in the target, which does not compile out of a borrow — so the read is cloned:
`return c.label` returns a copy in the source and the receiver survives, while the same text
in Rust moves out of `&self`.
zero_values is what a struct literal's OMITTED fields become. Go fills them with the field
type's zero and the target rejects an incomplete literal, so the engine spells them out. A
type with no entry refuses by name rather than falling back to `Default::default()`, which
would compile for these four and quietly mean something else for a type whose Default is not
its zero.
trait_object_forms is how a TRAIT reaches a value position. The source holds an interface
value directly and the target cannot — a trait has no size — so it arrives as `&dyn T`,
`Box<dyn T>`, `Rc<dyn T>` or a generic parameter, and those are different answers to who owns
the value and how long it lives. Only `param` is declared: a borrow is unambiguously right
there and the caller keeps the value. `result` is deliberately absent, so returning an
interface refuses by name rather than being boxed on a guess.
The supertrait position takes the bare path: an embedded interface becomes a trait BOUND, which
is the one place a trait appears as itself rather than as something holding it. Declared rather
than special-cased in the engine, so every position answers the same way.
failure_convention is what makes a function FALLIBLE. The source returns failure as a trailing
result of a designated type, checked by convention rather than enforced; the target expresses
it as the whole return type. Only the SOURCE side is declared here — which type carries the
convention and how the absent value is spelled — because `Result`, `Ok` and `Err` are target
spellings and the face that renders the target owns them.
The target type is a boxed trait object rather than a `thiserror` enum because the emitted
crate is compiled against the standard library alone. A real port declares its own error type
here and nothing in the engine changes.
function_map answers for a CALL the way type_map answers for a type, keyed by source identity
so a local named `errors` cannot be mistaken for the package. It is not optional for a real
package: every one calls its standard library, and the standard library is exactly the part
that does not come along. `len` casts because the source's `len` returns its `int`, which this
pack maps to `i64`, and the target's returns a `usize`.
A template brackets ITSELF where it needs to. The engine substitutes text and does not know
what the surrounding expression will be, so a template whose result binds looser than a caller
might is the template author's problem to parenthesise — the same contract type_constructors has.
The type map covers the source's WHOLE basic set, because a real package uses most of it in
its first file — a map sized to a fixture corpus is a map sized to what the engine already
handled. `int` and `int64` both take `i64` because the source's `int` is 64-bit on every
platform this programme targets; `rune` is a code point and takes `char`, not `i32`, because
the target has a type for exactly that and using it keeps the meaning.
The `untyped` rows are the source's UNTYPED CONSTANTS, which carry a default type rather than
a declared one. They are listed rather than folded into their defaults because they are
distinct identities in the front end and a table that answered for one and not the other would
resolve a constant and refuse the variable beside it.
complex64/128 map to a name the target does not have, ON PURPOSE. The target has no complex
type and inventing one silently would be worse than the compile error this produces; the row
exists so the failure names the type rather than reading as an unmapped-type hole.
`error` maps to the TRAIT, not to a boxed one. Where a trait may stand is a position question
the trait_object_forms table answers, so a parameter becomes `&dyn std::error::Error` and a
result — which the target must own — refuses until the pack declares how it is owned.
cast_types names the SOURCE types a conversion reaches by a plain cast. The source DEFINES numeric
conversion to truncate and the target's cast does the same thing, so the two agree and the cast is
faithful. A conversion the pack does not list is one where they disagree — string to byte slice is
infallible and lossy in the source and fallible in the target — and those refuse, because what
happens to input the target rejects is a decision rather than a spelling.
The `array` template uses `{name}`, which is the type's own non-type datum — for an array that
is its LENGTH. `[N]T` is a VALUE type that copies on assignment and carries its size in its
type; rendering it as a growable heap type changed all three at once, and none of the three is
visible in the emitted text.
`len` casts to the source width, and the INDEX casts back. Both are needed and neither is
redundant on its own: `return len(s)` wants the source's int, and `v[i]` wants the target's
usize, and the same value reaches both. Where a counter makes the round trip the pair is visible
and removable — which is why a cast is an IR node rather than text, so the right-sizing analysis
can see it and delete it rather than parse it out of a string.

copy_types names every source scalar whose target counterpart is Copy, so reading one is a read rather than a clone. It held only bool/int/float64, which is not a decision but an incomplete list: every other numeric width emitted a `.clone()` on a Copy value -- output that compiles and that no reviewer would accept. `string` is deliberately absent: it maps to an owned String, which is not Copy, so reading one really does clone.

zero_values held four entries -- bool, int, float64, string -- so every other scalar had no zero at all and any construction needing one refused. Not a decision, an incomplete list, the same shape the copy_types gap had. The composite kinds are keyed by KIND rather than by name because an unnamed type has none; `array` carries a template because its zero needs the ELEMENT's zero and the length, neither of which is knowable without the type tree.

literal_constructors says what a SEQUENCE literal becomes, keyed by the type's kind and given its elements already translated and comma-joined. Separate from type_constructors, which answers the same kinds for a TYPE position: `Vec<u8>` is what the type becomes and `vec![..]` is what the literal becomes, and one table answering both would have to know which it was being asked. A map is deliberately absent: the source's map literal has no order and the target's ordered map imposes one, so the entry order becomes observable where it was not -- a decision needing its own reason rather than a row here.

pointer_dispositions answers for a REFERENCE type too -- a map or a slice parameter -- because the source shares those with the caller exactly as it shares a pointer, and the facts that decide the form are the same facts. Only the form differs: a pointer's owned form is `Option<Box<T>>` because the source's pointer can be nil and the pointee needs an owner, and none of that is true of a sequence that is already owned. A disposition with no reference_target refuses for a reference, which is the honest answer for one that escapes or whose facts are unproven.

constant_map.reason: The source's PREDECLARED constants, which are identifiers rather than literals: `true` reaches the model as an ident referring to a universe-scope constant, not as a literal, so nothing in the literal path answers for it. Declared here rather than recognised in code for the same reason `type_map` is data: a source vocabulary the engine reads, not a decision the engine makes. `iota` is absent deliberately -- it is meaningful only inside a const declaration, where its value depends on position, and a table of names cannot say what it is. A predeclared constant the pack does not list refuses by name.

prose_type_names.reason: Source TYPE names that a doc comment may name, and the target's spelling for each. A reviewer reading a real ported package found 'the maximum value of a uint64' in prose beside a signature that correctly said `u64`, and said the code was translated and the documentation was not -- which was exactly right. A DELIBERATELY SMALL SET, and the bound is the substance: every name here is unambiguous in English, so a word matching one is naming a type. `string`, `bool`, `byte`, `int` and `error` are ABSENT for the opposite reason -- each is an ordinary English word, and rewriting 'returns a string of characters' into 'returns a String of characters' would make the prose worse to fix nothing. The full type map is not used for this and must not be: it exists to answer what a declaration's type BECOMES, where every entry is correct, and prose is not a declaration.

trait_receiver.reason: A Go interface says nothing about how an implementation binds its receiver, and the implementations are not all in view, so this cannot be recovered from the source — it can only be decided. EXCLUSIVE is the choice that does not silently forbid something: a shared receiver makes a mutating method like Named.Rename unimplementable, whereas an exclusive one only demands mutability from implementations that do not need it, which is a compile-time inconvenience rather than a lost capability. Revisit when the front end reports per-method mutation; see docs/programs/k8s-port/census/ownership-escape.md.

deferred_kinds.reason: An interface satisfaction whose concrete type this corpus does not declare — a standard-library value assigned where a standard-library interface is expected is the common case, and `var buf bytes.Buffer` passed as an `io.Writer` is the exact shape. There is nowhere to emit the impl: the type belongs to neither this corpus nor this crate, so the target's coherence rule forbids it outright. Recorded rather than dropped, because a satisfaction the engine cannot host must stay distinguishable from one that does not exist; deferred rather than refused, because refusing would reject every package that touches the standard library through an interface, which is most of them.

The source runs package init work before main, in dependency order across packages and file order within one, with no way to observe or defer it. The target has no such phase. LazyLock runs on first use rather than before it, which is a different program whenever the work has side effects or whenever two packages' initialisation order matters; an explicit init function called from main is faithful but changes the library's API and pushes the ordering obligation onto every caller. Choosing between them is a decision about the ported program's startup, not a spelling, so it is declared rather than inferred. Recorded as a declaration so the work is VISIBLE: it was reaching the model nowhere at all, which is neither a translation nor a refusal, and three of eight surveyed packages declare one.

undecided_forms.reason: A package-level var something WRITES is a mutable global, and the target has no immediate counterpart: `static` is immutable, `static mut` is unsafe, and `Mutex` imposes blocking the source never had, `RwLock` a reader/writer split it never stated, and an atomic exists only for some types. Each is a decision about the ported program's CONCURRENCY rather than a spelling, so none of them is a default this engine may pick. SCOPE, now that it can be measured: across the surveyed corpora most package variables are never written anywhere in their own package, and for those the form IS decided -- a `static`, because the source variable has one storage location and one address for the life of the program, a `const` is materialised afresh at every use and has no stable address, and an immutable `static` has exactly that storage identity with nothing to synchronize. This reason applies only to what remains. See docs/programs/k8s-port/census/ownership-escape.md and concurrency.md.

pointer_dispositions.reference_reason: THE APPEND PATTERN, and it is owned because the source says so. A sequence parameter the body REBINDS is a header the callee owns: rebinding it does not touch the caller's variable, and returning it is how the caller gets the new one back -- `dst = grow(dst, ..)` on both sides. So handing ownership over and returning it is exactly what the source does, not a cost imposed on the caller. Distinguished from the pass-through `return xs`, which does NOT rebind: there the source's caller keeps its slice and gets it back, so consuming it would take something the source never took. That one still refuses.

construction.reason: The parameter owns the value, so the argument hands ownership over. `Box::new` because taking the address in the source is what allocated it, and `Some` because the parameter carries the nil the source could hold. This MOVES the argument, which the source does not do -- and it is the cost the owned form already pays at the parameter. The argument site cannot pay a different one without the two disagreeing.

pointer_dispositions.reason: A sequence the body rebinds and returns is the source's append pattern, where the caller hands its slice over and takes the result back. Placed BEFORE the escaping rule because it is the more specific shape and rules are evaluated in declared order. ITS POINTER BEHAVIOUR IS DELIBERATELY IDENTICAL to that rule's: a disposition is matched on FACTS, so this one sees pointer parameters too, and only the REFERENCE form is what it exists to change. Giving it a pointer form of its own re-answered a question it was not asked -- which it did, until a coverage drop said so.

The pointer outlives the call — it is returned or captured — so no borrow can be handed out: a reference would need a lifetime the caller cannot supply. Owned is the form that is always available, and `Option` carries the nil the source could hold. NO RECEIVER FORM: a method whose receiver escapes cannot be a borrow of self, and refusing is better than picking a borrow that will not hold.

construction.reason: The parameter owns the value, so the argument hands ownership over. `Box::new` because taking the address in the source is what allocated it, and `Some` because the parameter carries the nil the source could hold. This MOVES the argument, which the source does not do -- and it is the cost the owned form already pays at the parameter. The argument site cannot pay a different one without the two disagreeing.

pointer_dispositions.reason: The pointer reached a call the front end did not analyse, so 'not mutated' and 'does not escape' are UNPROVEN rather than false. A borrow chosen on unproven facts is a guess; the owned form costs a move and cannot be wrong. Revisit when the analysis follows calls.

construction.reason: The same construction as `escaping_owned`, for a different reason: the facts are UNPROVEN rather than known, and the owned form was chosen because it cannot be wrong. The argument must match the parameter it feeds, so it moves too. Revisit when the analysis follows calls.

pointer_dispositions.reference_reason: A REFERENCE under unproven facts borrows SHARED, and the reasoning is not the pointer's. The owned form was chosen for a pointer because it costs a move and cannot be wrong -- and that escape hatch does not exist here: owning a map, a slice or a string CONSUMES the caller's value, which the source never does, so owned is not the safe answer but a wrong one. Of what remains, a shared borrow is the only choice that neither consumes nor narrows. `&mut` would demand exclusive access the source never demanded and would fail at the CALLER. And a shared borrow that turns out to be insufficient -- because the body hands the reference to a callee that mutates through it -- does not compile. That is the difference that decides it: an unproven borrow on a reference fails LOUDLY at the port, where an owned parameter would have silently changed what the program does to its caller's value. Revisit when the analysis can read the effects of the standard library, which is what leaves these facts unproven; `census/` sizes no such family yet.

pointer_dispositions.reason: The body provably assigns through this pointer and nothing outlives the call, so an exclusive borrow is what the code does. This is a HYPOTHESIS about aliasing, not a proof: escape analysis shows lifetime compatibility and not the exclusivity a borrow needs, because a Go caller may pass one pointer as two arguments. What makes it safe to emit is that the target checks it — an unsatisfiable `&mut` is a borrow-check error the compile proof catches, which is a red build rather than silent corruption. See docs/programs/k8s-port/census/ownership-escape.md.

construction.reason: The parameter is an exclusive borrow, so the argument lends exclusively. Nothing moves and the caller keeps the value, which is what the source does.

pointer_dispositions.reference_reason: The body writes through the reference and nothing outlives the call, so an exclusive borrow is what the code does -- and it is what the SOURCE does too: a map parameter shares the caller's map, and writing an element of a slice parameter is visible to the caller through the shared backing.

pointer_dispositions.reason: Nothing mutates through it and nothing outlives the call, so a shared borrow is both sufficient and the cheapest form. Same aliasing caveat as the exclusive case, and much weaker: a shared borrow coexists with other shared borrows, so caller-side aliasing does not invalidate it.

construction.reason: The parameter is a shared borrow, so the argument lends. Nothing moves and the caller keeps the value.

pointer_dispositions.reference_reason: The body only reads, so a shared borrow carries exactly what the source's reference carried: the caller keeps the value and sees it unchanged. Emitting an owned parameter here would consume the caller's map or slice, which the source never does.

trait_object_forms._reason: A PARAMETER of interface type is generic, not dynamic. The source's interface parameter is a dynamic value because the source has no other kind; the target has both, and `&impl Trait` is what it writes for a parameter — it accepts every implementor exactly as the source's does, monomorphises rather than dispatching through a table, and needs no allocation. `&dyn Trait` buys heterogeneity a PARAMETER cannot use: one call passes one value, and a caller that needs a mixed collection builds one at its own boundary. Reviewers named `&dyn` at every interface boundary as a port artifact, and they were right: it is the shape you get by mapping the source's one kind of interface value onto the target's one that resembles it, rather than onto the one a parameter wants. A RESULT still has no declared form and still refuses. Returning an interface needs an owner, and `impl Trait` in return position names a single hidden type where the source's result may be a different one on every path -- which is a different program, not a different spelling.

failure_convention.reason: The source's error is an interface value; the target's is a trait object, and a trait object needs an owner because it has no size. Boxed rather than borrowed: a failure outlives the call that produced it, so a reference would need a lifetime the caller cannot supply. SEND + SYNC IS NOT DECORATION. Without them the ported error cannot cross a thread boundary or enter any async runtime, which does not merely inconvenience a caller -- it makes the emitted crate unusable in concurrent code, where the source's error had no such limit. A reviewer reading the emitted API named this as breaking the crate for concurrent use, and they were right: the bound was missing, not declined. The source's own error values are ordinary data and satisfy both bounds; a source error that did not would not be shareable across the source's goroutines either. ON THE CRITICISM THAT A CONSUMER CANNOT MATCH ON IT, raised by two reviewers reading the emitted crate: that is the SOURCE's error model, carried across rather than introduced. The source's `errors.New("empty")` gives its own callers exactly as little -- an opaque interface value with a string inside -- and a source caller who wants to branch uses `errors.Is`/`errors.As` against a sentinel value or a concrete type, which is what the target's boxed trait object plus a downcast supports. A concrete error enum would give the ported crate an API the source does not have. That is an IMPROVEMENT on the source, and improving is not porting: it invents a type upstream never declared, it cannot represent a failure propagated from a callee the package does not know, and the next upstream release would have to be reconciled against a shape nobody upstream wrote. The engine's job is to carry the source's design, including where that design is poor -- and to say so here rather than silently be blamed for it.
failure_convention.discard_reason: A failing return in the source carries the value beside the failure and the target's carries only the failure, so the companion has nowhere to go. The source DOCUMENTS that when a function returns a non-nil error its other results are not guaranteed to be meaningful, so dropping the companion is faithful to the convention -- and refusing unless the value could be seen to be inert was faithful only to the cases inspection could confirm, which left most real fallible code unported. THE COST: a source program that violates its own convention -- writing a meaningful value beside a failure and having its caller read it -- ports to a target program that does not carry that value, and the engine cannot tell such a program from a conforming one because the difference lives in the caller. THE CASE THAT GIVES MOST PAUSE: a NAMED result may have been written through before the failure, so the value is work a reader can see happening and cannot see being discarded. Under the convention it is still unreadable, so the same argument covers it -- but it is where a reader would most reasonably expect otherwise, which is why it is named here. Set to false to return to refusing, which costs coverage and buys correctness for programs that break their own contract.
failure_convention.constructor_reason: Which callees PRODUCE a failure, and therefore never produce the absent value. Needed because the target's failing return is `Err(..)` and the source's is a value that MAY be absent: wrapping an error-typed expression in `Err` is right only when that expression cannot be nil, and wrong -- silently, at runtime, in the direction of reporting failure where the source reported success -- when it can. `func (r *Report) Cause() error` returning a stored field is the shape that shows it: the source's caller checks the result against nil, and a target that always returns `Err` is a different program. A CALL to one of these is proof, because a failure constructor has no nil result to return. The other proof the engine has needs no table: the ADDRESS OF A FRESH COMPOSITE is never nil. An error-typed expression that is neither refuses by name. Add a callee here only when it cannot return the absent value on any path.
failure_convention.sentinel_reason: A SENTINEL is a package-level failure value the source declares once and returns from many places: `var ErrSize = errors.New("size")`. It is the commonest error-typed package variable in real code and it blocks twice over -- the declaration is not a constant expression, and every `return ErrSize` is an operand nothing can prove is a failure. THE DECISION: a sentinel becomes a TYPE. A unit struct that implements `Display` with the source's message and implements the target's error trait, so `Err(ErrSize.into())` is a failure a caller can compare against. IT BECAME A TYPE RATHER THAN ITS MESSAGE, and that is a reversal worth recording. The message form -- `static ERR_SIZE: &str` with the failure built from it at each return -- was correct and cheaper, and it lost the one thing that makes a sentinel a sentinel: the source's caller writes `errors.Is(err, ErrSize)` and compares IDENTITY, and a fresh failure built from a shared message is equal to nothing. The port was strictly less capable than the source, and five reviewers said so in different words before the cost was paid. WHAT THIS IS NOT: an error enum. Reviewers asked for one repeatedly and a real package cannot have it -- measured on `semver`, an enum generated from its seven sentinels would cover 16 of 78 failure sites, because 43 are built by `fmt.Errorf` with a formatted message and have no variant to be. A `#[non_exhaustive]` enum that silently omits four fifths of what a caller can receive is a WORSE API than the boxed trait object, not a better one. The source's failure set is not closed, and an engine may not close it on the author's behalf. What would change that: a source package whose every failure IS a declared sentinel has a closed set and deserves the enum. Measured across the surveyed corpora, that is none of them.
failure_convention.alias_reason: The failure type is the longest thing in most emitted signatures and it appears in every fallible one -- `Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync>`, spelled out eight times in a four-hundred-line module. Reviewers named it twice: the type is repeated where any author writing it a third time would have introduced an alias. So a unit with a fallible declaration emits one: `pub type Result<T> = std::result::Result<T, <target_type>>;`, and its signatures name it. This changes the SPELLING and not the program -- an alias is transparent, so a caller may still write the full type and the two are the same. PER UNIT rather than per crate, because the engine emits one module per source package and has no crate root of its own to put it in; a module-scoped `Result` is what a crate organised that way writes anyway. Emitted only where the unit HAS a fallible declaration, so a module that never fails does not gain a name it never uses. Set to empty to spell the type out at every site.
failure_convention.inferred_construction_reason: How a failure value is built where the DESTINATION already fixes its type -- inside the target's failing return, which is the only place the engine builds one. The general mapping for the source's failure constructor is explicit about the type, and its reason says why: it fires in any position, and an inferring conversion only works where the destination type is already known. Inside `Err(..)` of a function whose return type names the failure, it IS known -- so the explicit form there is a turbofish that says something the signature has already said, which a reviewer reading the emitted crate called noise twice. Set to empty to use the general form everywhere, which is what the engine did before and is still correct -- just longer.
failure_convention.identity_test_reason: How a caller asks whether a failure IS a particular sentinel. The source writes `err == ErrSize` or `errors.Is(err, ErrSize)` and compares identity; the target asks the trait object what concrete type it holds. This exists because the sentinel became a TYPE. While a sentinel was its message, there was nothing to compare -- a fresh failure built from a shared string is equal to nothing -- and the comparison REFUSED by name, with the loss recorded as the cost of that decision. The type restores it, and this is the form that spends it. Faithful in the direction that matters: the source's comparison is true exactly when the failure is that sentinel, and so is this. The one difference is what happens to a WRAPPED failure -- the source's `errors.Is` walks an unwrap chain and a downcast does not -- so a package that wraps its sentinels and tests them through the wrapper gets a test that says no where the source said yes. Recorded rather than hidden: no surveyed corpus does it, and the answer when one does is a chain the emitted failure type does not currently carry.
failure_convention.param_type_reason: What the failure type is as a PARAMETER, which is the one interface position where the general form is wrong. Every other interface parameter is `&impl Trait`: it accepts every implementor, monomorphises, and needs no table. A FAILURE parameter is different because of what callers do with it -- they ask which sentinel it is, and that question is `downcast_ref`, which exists on the trait OBJECT and not on a generic. `&impl Error` accepts the value and then cannot answer the only question anyone asks of it. `'static` because downcasting requires it, and the source's error values are owned data that borrow nothing. `Send + Sync` are absent here on purpose: the owned form needs them so a ported failure can cross a thread boundary, and a BORROW of one crossing nothing does not, so requiring them of every caller's error would narrow the parameter for no gain.
failure_convention.sentinel_prefix_reason: The prefix the source puts on a sentinel's NAME, which the target drops. `var ErrEmptyString` is prefixed because the source has no namespacing inside a package and every sentinel would otherwise collide with an ordinary name; the target has modules, so `semver::EmptyString` says everything `semver::ErrEmptyString` does. And the prefix actively hurts there: the target's failure arm is literally called `Err`, so `Err(ErrEmptyString)` stutters at every return -- a reviewer named exactly that. Dropped only where the sentinel is one this engine PROVED, so the prefix is known to be the convention rather than part of a name; only where what is left is not empty; and only where nothing else the unit declares already answers to it, because a rename that collides is worse than a stutter. Set to empty to keep the source's name.
failure_convention.target_type_alternative_reason: WHY NOT AN ENUM. Three independent blind reviewers led with this, each proposing that the unit's sentinels become one `#[non_exhaustive] enum`. It is a better Rust API and it is a DIFFERENT API from the one being ported, and the difference is measured rather than asserted. (1) An enum cannot type a parameter that accepts an ARBITRARY failure. The source's error is an open interface, and 16 parameters across the seven surveyed packages take one -- 10 in `errors` and 4 in `multierror`, two packages that exist for no other purpose. A per-unit enum would accept only failures that unit declares, so those signatures become untypeable: not a worse API, an impossible one. (2) An enum built from a unit's sentinels does not cover its failures. `semver` declares 7 sentinels and has 78 failure sites; the enum reaches 16 of them, and 43 are formatted messages with no variant to be. (3) Adding a `Message(String)` variant for those gives a caller nothing the box does not, and the enum must be `#[non_exhaustive]` regardless -- so there is no exhaustiveness benefit either, which was the whole argument for it. What the reviewers were seeing is real and is a different thing: in a PARTIAL port the sentinel types are constructed and never compared, because the functions that compare them refused. The comparison is emitted -- `corpus-sentinel` proves it -- and appears as those functions land.
failure_convention.sentinel_enum_reason: The ONE type a unit's proved sentinels become, as variants. Empty to give each its own type. Two decisions were conflated here for a long time, and separating them is what made this possible. `target_type` is what a fallible function RETURNS, and it has to stay the open boxed one because the source's error is an open interface -- 16 parameters across the surveyed corpus accept an arbitrary failure, and a closed type cannot express those at all. But that says nothing about how a unit's OWN declared sentinels are spelled, and spelling them as one type per sentinel was a separate choice that never had to follow. Grouping preserves everything the separate types carried: distinct identity per sentinel, the message each holds, and the comparison a caller makes -- and it still boxes at the boundary, so an arbitrary failure crosses exactly as before. What it removes is seven near-identical blocks of `struct` + `Display` + `Error`, which three independent reviewers named as their single most decisive evidence that nobody wrote this by hand. NAMED for what it is rather than after the package, because the target addresses it through the module already: `semver::Error` says everything `semver::SemverError` does. Falls back to one type per sentinel where the unit already declares this name, because a collision is worse than the boilerplate.
failure_convention.sentinel_enum_exhaustive_reason: Whether a caller outside the crate may match the enum exhaustively. FALSE, so the emitted type carries `#[non_exhaustive]`: the source's sentinel set is a package's own list and grows without ceremony there, where in the target an added variant would break every downstream match. The cost is stated: an exhaustive `match` was part of what reviewers wanted from an enum, and this withholds it. Taken anyway because a library that cannot add a failure without a major version is a worse outcome than one whose callers write a wildcard arm.
failure_convention.identity_test_grouped_reason: How identity is tested when the sentinels are GROUPED. `{0}` is the failure, `{1}` the enum, `{2}` the variant. Two questions where the ungrouped form asked one -- is this failure that type, and is it that variant -- because grouping makes the type shared and the variant the discriminator. An EQUALITY rather than a pattern match, for a reason about the emitted text rather than the semantics: the two say the same thing and the enum derives the comparison either way, but a `matches!` is a macro, and the target's formatter prints macro bodies as raw tokens -- `downcast_ref::< Error > ()` with spaces nobody types. A form that formats is worth more than one that saves a derive the type already has.

errors.New.reason: The source's error is an interface value carrying a message; the target's is a boxed trait object. `from` on a string is the constructor that exists for it, and boxing is what gives the trait object a size. The alternative -- a concrete error type per call site -- would invent a type the source does not have. The turbofish is explicit rather than `.into()`: this mapping fires in any position, and `.into()` only infers where the destination type is already known -- correct inside `Err(..)` and ambiguous inside a `let`.

len.reason: The source's `len` yields its own `int`, which the pack maps to `i64`; the target's yields `usize`. The cast is in the VALUE position because the value is what the source typed as `int` -- and the index position casts back, because the same value reaches both. Where a counter makes the round trip the pair is visible and removable by a right-sizing analysis, which is why a cast is an IR node rather than characters in a string.

panic.reason: Go's `panic(v)` aborts the goroutine carrying `v`; Rust's `panic!` unwinds carrying a formatted string. Where `v` is a STRING LITERAL the two are the same abort with the same message and the same payload type, and nothing is lost -- which is why this mapping declares that shape and refuses every other one by name. Where `v` is an error or an arbitrary value, the payload TYPE is lost, and a caller that recovers and type-asserts on it sees a different program. ON EMITTING A PANIC AT ALL: the no-panic bar governs THIS repository's own Rust, and the engine's production sources contain none. The emitted crate's semantics come from upstream: a source function that aborts must port to a target function that aborts, and returning a `Result` where the source panics would be a different program -- which is the one failure this engine exists to prevent. Sized by docs/programs/k8s-port/census/defer-panic-recover.md: the string-literal invariant shapes are 38.2% and 21.0% of Kubernetes panic sites.

length_functions.reason: Callees whose value IS a length. The source types them as its own `int`, which the type map sends to `i64` — right for a value the source typed `int`, and wrong for a length, which the target types `usize`. Named here rather than recognised in code so a pack for another source language names its own and the engine names none. A function returning nothing but one of these returns a LENGTH, and the conversion the call's mapping adds exists only to make the value type as the source's `int`: where the value never is one, the conversion is what is wrong. Equivalent because a length is the same set of values in both — the source's cannot be negative and cannot exceed what the target's `usize` holds.

integer_arithmetic.reason: The source defines signed and unsigned overflow as WRAPPING; the target panics on overflow in a debug build and wraps in a release one. Emitting the plain operator therefore turns one source program into two target programs, neither of which is it -- output that compiles and means something different is the failure this engine exists to prevent. FOUR INDEPENDENT REVIEWERS have called this out, each saying the same true thing: no Rust author reaches for `wrapping_add` on `self.calls += 1`, and the spelling disables the debug check that would have caught a bug. The objection is right about intent and wrong about what the engine may do with it -- the engine cannot read intent, and the source's guarantee is not conditional on the author having wanted it. THREE ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED AND REJECTED, recorded so this stops being re-litigated. (1) Emit the plain operator and accept the debug panic: that is a different program for every input that overflows, and the programs where wrapping is load-bearing -- a hash mixer is the obvious one -- would abort instead of returning. (2) Type the ported values as the target's own wrapping newtype, so the plain operator carries the rule: this reads naturally at the operation and infects every signature, field and caller with a wrapper the source does not have, which is a larger unfaithfulness than the one it fixes. (3) Have the emitted crate turn overflow checks off in its own build profile: a profile setting does not reach a crate's DEPENDENTS, so a ported library used as a dependency would still be built under the consumer's profile and would still panic. WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER: a proof that a particular operation cannot overflow. The engine has one such proof already -- a division whose operands make overflow impossible keeps the plain operator -- and every further one narrows this by construction rather than by taste. A range analysis over the source is the shape of the next one, and there is no census sizing it.

doc_convention.reason: The source's convention requires a doc comment to open with the identifier it documents; the target's requires that it does not, and writes in the third person. Copying the source form verbatim is what makes emitted documentation read as translated rather than written -- flagged on every doc comment by a reviewer who did not know the code was generated, as the loudest single signal a Rust developer had not written it. The rewrite is mechanical and bounded: the leading word must equal the declaration's own source name EXACTLY, and a copula immediately following it is dropped with it so `ID is an alias` becomes `An alias` rather than the ungrammatical `Is an alias`. A doc that opens any other way is left exactly as written, because its author already chose an opening and this has no business rewording prose it was not asked about.

derives.name: Debug
derives.reason: Every source value can be printed by the source's own formatting verbs, so a ported type that cannot be printed at all has lost something the source had. Without it nothing emitted can appear in an assertion, a log line, or any bound asking for `Debug` -- which is most of them.

derives.name: Clone
derives.reason: The source copies a struct on assignment, so every source struct is duplicable. `Clone` is the target's name for that, made explicit at each use rather than implicit at every assignment.

derives.name: Default
derives.reason: EVERY source type has a zero value and `var x T` produces it, so a default is a fact about the source rather than an invention. A trait object has no zero, which is why one blocks this.

derives.name: PartialEq
derives.reason: The source compares structs with `==` exactly when no field is a slice, a map or a function -- and those are precisely the fields whose target counterpart is not comparable either. The two languages agree here, so this is derived rather than guessed: a type the source could compare, the port can compare.

derives.name: Eq
derives.reason: TOTAL equality, which the source has wherever `==` is defined and no field is a float. The float is the whole of the difference and it is not a conservative exclusion: NaN is not equal to itself in EITHER language, so a struct with a float field has no equivalence relation in either, and claiming one in the target would be claiming something the source never had. Everything `PartialEq` blocks blocks this too, because a type with no partial equality has no total equality.

derives.name: Hash
derives.reason: The source's requirement for a MAP KEY is that the type be comparable, and the target spells that requirement `Eq + Hash`. A source type usable as a map key must port to one usable as a target map key, or a ported program that indexes by it has nowhere to go — and a reviewer reading the emitted crate said exactly that of a point type whose fields all support both. Blocked by the same set as `Eq`, because `Hash` without `Eq` violates a contract the target's own documentation states: equal values must hash equally, and a type with no equality cannot promise it.

idioms.reason: The source spells the emptiness test as a comparison against the empty string literal, and the target has a method for it. Exactly equivalent -- both are true precisely when the value has length zero -- so this changes the spelling and not the program. `clippy::style` flags the comparison form, which is what makes it a review comment on hand-written code and therefore a defect in emitted code held to that bar. Applies to `==` and to `!=`, the second negated.

A struct literal field whose value is a binding of the SAME name is written without the colon in the target. Exactly equivalent -- the shorthand is defined as the long form -- so this changes the spelling and not the program. `clippy::style` flags the long form as `redundant_field_names`, and a comment a reviewer would make on hand-written code is a defect in code held to that bar. The source has no shorthand and therefore always writes the long form, so this fires wherever a constructor passes a parameter straight into the field it names -- which is what most constructors do.

A BORROWED sequence parameter is spelled as a slice rather than as a borrow of the owned container. `&[T]` accepts every `&Vec<T>` and also an array, a boxed slice and a subrange, so it takes strictly more callers while promising strictly less -- which is why `clippy::style` flags the container form as `ptr_arg`. Nothing about the program changes: the parameter is borrowed either way, and the source's slice was never an owned container in the first place. It is composed structurally rather than by rewriting the spelling -- the disposition's borrow template substitutes `[element]` where it would have substituted the resolved container -- so a re-spelled container type cannot silently stop matching.

Inside a type's own impl block the target spells that type `Self`. Exactly equivalent -- `Self` IS the implementing type -- so this changes the spelling and not the program, and `clippy::style` flags the repetition as `use_self`. It matters more than repetition usually does because `Self` survives a rename: a constructor written `-> Self { Self { .. } }` keeps working when the type is renamed, and one written with the name twice has two places to miss. The source has no such spelling and therefore always writes the name, so every constructor the engine moves onto a type would otherwise carry it twice.

The source counts with its `int` and the target indexes with `usize`, so the engine converts at both ends: `for i in 0..values.len() as i64` and then `values[i as usize]`. Where the counter is used for NOTHING BUT indexing, the signed value is never observed and both conversions are removable -- the counter is a `usize` from the start. Exactly equivalent, because the round trip is the identity for every value the loop can produce: the range's upper bound IS a length, so no value in it can be negative or exceed `usize`. This changes the spelling and not the program, which is what makes it an idiom rather than a rule. A reviewer reading the emitted crate called the pair 'a length cast to signed and immediately cast back to index, with bounds checks the iterator would have elided', and they are right about the first half; the second is a further step this does not take. Applies only where every read of the counter inside the loop is an index operand. One read that is not -- passed to a function, compared against something the source typed `int`, stored -- and the signed value IS observed, so the conversions stay.

`for i := 0; i < len(xs); i++ { .. xs[i] .. }` counts in order to reach each element, because the source has no other way to walk a sequence by value. The target does, and iterating it is the same walk: the same elements, in the same order, exactly as many times. What goes is the counter, which existed only to be an index. EQUIVALENT rather than merely shorter, and the bound is what makes it so: the loop runs from zero to the sequence's own length, so every index it produces is in range and every element is reached once. A loop whose bound is anything else is not this shape and keeps its counter. `clippy::needless_range_loop` names this on hand-written Rust, which is what makes the index form a review comment on hand-written code and therefore a defect in emitted code held to that bar -- and it is the finding three independent reviewers reached for first. THE ELEMENT NEEDS A NAME AND THE SOURCE GIVES NONE, which is the one thing this rule invents. It is a loop-local binding: no caller can see it, nothing outside the loop depends on it, and the alternative is keeping a counter the target does not need. The convention is the sequence's own name with a trailing plural `s` removed, so `values` yields `value` -- and where that yields nothing usable, or collides with a name the body already binds, the rule does not fire and the counter stays. An invented name that shadows a real one would be a different program.

`a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]` is an EXCHANGE, and the target's sequence has a method for exactly it. The parallel assignment is already faithful -- both sides are evaluated before either is written, which is what makes it an exchange rather than two writes -- so this changes the spelling and not the program. Recognised STRUCTURALLY and narrowly: two places and two values, each place an index into the same sequence, and the values the same two indices in the opposite order. Anything else is a parallel assignment that happens to have two of each, and keeps its own form. Three independent reviewers named the destructuring form as hand-rolling a method the target has had since 1.0, which is what makes the long form a review comment on hand-written code and therefore a defect in emitted code held to that bar.

A function whose every return is -1, 0 or 1 is a THREE-WAY COMPARISON, and the source has no other way to spell one: its sort and its comparison interfaces are defined in terms of a signed integer. The target has a type for exactly this, and it is the type its own sorting and its own `Ord` are defined in terms of. The integer form is not merely unidiomatic in the target, it is the bug class the type was introduced to remove: every consumer has to re-derive which way round the sign goes, and a sign convention inverted somewhere in that chain compiles and sorts backwards. A reviewer reading a real ported package said so of `compare_segment` before knowing anything about where it came from. EQUIVALENT because the three values are the whole range: a function that can return anything else is not this shape and keeps its integer. Applies only where every return is one of the three literals -- a returned VARIABLE could hold anything, and proving otherwise is a range analysis this does not have. AND THE LADDER GOES WITH IT where the branches are the comparison itself: `if v < o { Less } if v > o { Greater } Equal` over one pair of operands is what the target's `cmp` returns, and the ladder exists in the source only because it has no such method. A reviewer put it exactly: the ladder is NECESSARY there and dead here.

A match whose arms yield only `true` and `false` is a membership TEST, and the target has a macro that is exactly one: `matches!(x, "x" | "*" | "X")`. The source has to spell it as a switch because its switch is the only multi-pattern form it has. Exactly equivalent -- the macro expands to the match -- so this changes the spelling and not the program, which is what makes it an idiom. `clippy::match_like_matches_macro` names it on hand-written Rust, which is what makes the long form a review comment on hand-written code and therefore a defect in emitted code held to that bar. Applies where the DEFAULT arm yields `false` and every other yields `true`; the reverse is a negated membership test and needs its own form, so it keeps the match rather than being silently inverted.

fmt.Sprintf.reason: The source builds a string from a template and arguments; the target's macro does exactly that and yields the same owned string. Nothing wraps it -- the value IS the result.

fmt.Errorf.reason: The same template, then the failure type this pack already carries for a constructed error. Spelled with the turbofish rather than `.into()` for the reason `errors.New` is: this fires in any position, and inference only has a destination type inside `Err(..)`. Note what this DOES NOT preserve: the source's `%w` records a cause that callers walk, and the wrap verb refuses for exactly that reason -- so every call that reaches this one builds a message and nothing else, which is what the source's other verbs do too.

format_calls.verbs_reason: The CLOSED set of source format verbs whose target placeholder means the same thing. `%v`, `%s` and `%d` all render a value in its default form, which is what `{}` does. `%q` renders a quoted, escaped string, which is what `{:?}` does for one. Everything else refuses BY NAME rather than defaulting to `{}`, because the ones left out differ in what they PRINT: `%x` is a base, `%T` is a type name the target has no runtime access to, `%+v` and `%#v` are Go-specific value dumps with no counterpart, and any width, precision or flag is a layout the target spells differently. A verb rendered as the wrong thing produces a program that compiles and prints something else, which is the failure this engine exists to prevent.
format_calls.wrap_verb_reason: `%w` is not a rendering at all -- it records the argument as the new error's CAUSE, which is what `errors.Is` and `errors.Unwrap` then walk. The target's `format!` produces a string and keeps no cause, so rendering `%w` as `{}` would compile, print the same text, and silently drop a chain callers navigate. Refused by name until the pack decides what a wrapped cause becomes.
format_calls.literal_only_reason: The template must be a STRING LITERAL. The target's `format!` is a macro that parses its template at compile time; a template computed at run time cannot be passed to it at all. The source allows either, so this is a real restriction and it is stated rather than worked around -- the alternative would be a runtime formatter that is a different mechanism with different behaviour.
format_calls.brace_reason: A literal brace in the source template is data; in the target's it opens a placeholder. Doubling it is how the target spells one, and skipping that would turn a message containing `{` into a parse error or, worse, into a placeholder that consumes an argument meant for something else.
format_calls.macro_reason: The target's macro that builds an owned string from a template. Named here rather than in code because it is the target's spelling for the source's operation, and every other such spelling in this pack is data.
format_calls.wrapper_reason: The target CALLEE that receives the formatted string, or empty when the string is the result. A callee path rather than a text template with a hole in it: the formatted value is a structured expression, and substituting one into text is what made every real formatting call in the corpus refuse -- its arguments are field reads and calls, which have no unambiguous text spelling.
